# The many faces of Wiraqucha

No important name has only one face. **Wiraqucha** appears as ​a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and a digital temple. This post looks at each face in turn: the name and ‌its roots, the Incan transcription original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the symbols and sanctuaries, and the afterlife that brought the canonical spelling into the present.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Wiraqucha
- **ASCII form:** ‌viracocha
- **Meaning:** "Sea of fat"
- **Domain of influence:** Creator, Sky, Sea Foam
- **Pantheon:** Incan
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Wiraqucha** (*viracocha*) — Creator, Sky, Sea Foam · Sea of fat — belongs to ​the Incan tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Creator, Sky, Sea Foam". The name means "Sea of fat".

**Wiraqucha** is the maker of the Inca cosmos: sky father, creator of ​sun and moon, and the weeping wanderer who once walked the length of the Andes and was never seen again. The chroniclers knew him as the invisible god who made the ​world and then withdrew from it — and his name still survives in the politest word an Andean elder can offer a stranger: *wiraqucha*, sir, gentleman, lord.

## Mythology

The stories of Wiraqucha place creator, sky, sea foam at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Wiraqucha appears ​in incan tradition as creator, sky, sea foam. The name's meaning, "Sea of fat", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Wiraqucha in ​ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Wiraqucha survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers ​— poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Wiraqucha gives the figure a ‌stable name around which these variants orbit.

### The Flood of Unu Pachakuti (Betanzos ch. 1)

Juan de Betanzos, whose *Suma y Narración de los Incas* (1551) is the fullest early account, ​tells that Wiraqucha made the first people at Tiwanaku and gave them the world to keep; but they grew proud and lived without worship, so he resolved to undo them. He sent ‌a great flood — *unu pachakuti*, a watery overturning of the world — that drowned the first race, the wari, while he himself rose into the sky above Titicaca. Yet he spared ​two, a man and a woman, calling them from the waters onto a float of totora reeds near the island, and commissioning them as the ancestors of a new humanity. The myth ‌fixes the shape of Andean time: catastrophe and renewal in cycles, a world unmade and remade, with the creator always watching from above. It is also a charter for the lake itself ​— Titicaca is not scenery but the hinge where the first world ended and the second began.

### The Making of Nations at Tiwanaku (Cobo 13.3)

Father Bernabé Cobo's *Historia del Nuevo ‌Mundo* (Book 13) preserves the imperial version: after the flood, Wiraqucha set to work at Tiwanaku, where he sculpted the forms of all the nations to come — each with its own ​face, dress, language, songs, and seeds — and brought them to life. When the work was done he dispatched them, calling them out of caves, springs, and rivers to find their homelands: ‌one nation he sent by way of a cave, another along a river's course, and to the Inca ancestors he gave the special charge that would lead them at last to Cusco. ​Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa's *Historia Indica* (ch. 6–7) gives the same program and adds the full titulature: Ticci Uiracocha Pachayachachic, 'ancient foundation, creator of the world.' The myth is a map of ​the Andes read backward — every people is the deliberate work of the same hand, and the Inca are simply the nation that remembered best who made them.

### The Sun, Moon, and ‌Stars (Sarmiento ch. 7)

The same accounts make Wiraqucha the maker of the sky. On the island of Titicaca in the great lake he fashioned the Sun — Inti — and ‌the Moon, and set the stars in their courses, appointing the Sun the most honored of all, 'like a rich ornament' among the rest (Sarmiento de Gamboa, ch. 7; Cobo 13.3). In ‌imperial theology Inti then became the visible ancestor of the Inca dynasties, while Wiraqucha remained the invisible maker behind the visible god — a two-tier heaven in which the sun was, as ​it were, the son, and the emperor the sun's line. The pairing let Cusco worship a present, national god without ever forgetting the older, unbounded one above and behind him. It is ​one of the few world mythologies in which the supreme creator deliberately steps back from the machinery of daily rule, delegating the visible sky to his own workmanship and reserving for himself ‌only the authorship of everything.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Wiraqucha concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The ​restored form Wiraqucha, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Creator, Sky, Sea Foam

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Wiraqucha across media and centuries. ​The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Wiraqucha carries the same precision in textual form.

- **Sea foam of the ‌lake** — The etymon wira-qucha, 'foam (or fat) of the lake' — the foam from which the name, and the god, emerged
- **The staff and traveler's bundle** — He crossed the Andes ​as a staff-carrying beggar, weeping at springs and prophesying — the god as itinerant stranger
- **The reed float** — The totora-reed float that bore the two survivors of the flood — the ​seed of the remade world
- **The stone models of Tiwanaku** — The sculpted prototypes of every nation, from which Wiraqucha shaped humankind at his workshop
- **The golden image of Cusco** — The ‌solid-gold statue in the Coricancha, described by Cobo and Murúa and melted down within years of the conquest

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus ​is yet assigned to Wiraqucha with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Incan name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence ‌remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Wiraqucha, sanctuary or cult remains tied to ​creator and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## A Meditation

Wiraqucha is the absent creator — ​the maker who finished his work, wept once over what was coming, and left. Andean theology has no jealous guardian and no returning savior: the world was handed over, and what happens ‌in it is, up to a point, the world's own business. That withdrawal is the deepest note in his mythology. Where other high gods demand attention, Wiraqucha demands only remembrance — his ‌name spoken in honorifics, his lake crossed at the solstice, his ruined workshop kept as pilgrimage ground.

And the weeping is the detail that keeps scholars returning. A god who cries at ‌a spring, foretelling bearded men in his own dress, is a god who has read the ending of the story he began. The chronicles that preserve the scene were written under colonial ‌rule, which should make us careful — but even as colonial construction it is extraordinary: a conquered people explaining the conquest in the voice of their own god, who saw it ​coming and left before it arrived. Absence, prophecy, grief: the maker's last gifts were the ones no one could take.
